title: Startup Guide to Inclusive Hiring Practices (October 2026)
summary: October 2026 guide to inclusive hiring practices that help startups build diverse teams through fair sourcing and interviews.
body_markdown:
Your job post asks for startup experience, a degree, and a career without gaps. Some of those filters may be screening out people who can do the work before you ever speak with them. You can build[inclusive hiring practices](https://www.dover.com/) around a simpler test: which requirements matter on day one, and how can each candidate fairly show they meet them?


**TLDR:**


-


Remove unnecessary credentials from your job criteria before reviewing applicants.


-


Broaden sourcing beyond referrals through community colleges and return-to-work programs.


-


Allow interview accommodations while keeping job-relevant assessment criteria consistent.


-


Use shared questions, anchored scorecards, and independent feedback before group discussion.


-


Review AI screening for unfair exclusions; keep humans responsible for hiring decisions.


## What Inclusive Hiring Practices Mean


Unnecessary hiring requirements can exclude capable candidates. Inclusive hiring practices remove barriers throughout recruitment so candidates can show job-relevant abilities fairly.


DEI means diversity, equity, and inclusion: team differences, fair access to opportunity, and meaningful participation. Accommodations may differ while assessment criteria stay consistent.


> DEI is not a separate category of candidate qualifications.


The goal is broader access and evidence-based selection, such as scoring job-relevant work samples instead of screening by school name, without demographic preferences or guaranteed representation outcomes.


## Why Inclusive Hiring Matters for Startups


Founder-only networks, informal interviews, and credential filters can sideline qualified applicants, including those from[non-tech backgrounds](https://www.dover.com/blog/why-hiring-from-non-tech-backgrounds-is-critical-to-your-startups-success) , before skills get tested. Inclusive hiring practices can widen access, clarify decisions, and build candidate trust.


BLS’s 2025 disability workforce report provides context:


Population Employment-population ratio


With disabilities 22.8%


Without disabilities 65.2%


These figures neither prove hiring discrimination nor measure available startup talent. They also mix all age groups: about half of people with a disability are 65 or older, which lowers the overall ratio, though BLS reports[the gap persists across all age groups](https://www.bls.gov/news.release/disabl.nr0.htm) . Annual estimates exclude October because data were not collected due to the 2025 federal government shutdown.


## Set Job-Relevant Criteria Before Recruiting


Before sourcing, document core responsibilities, observable skills, pay range, and the hiring decision owner. Separate job requirements from preferences for prestigious companies, uninterrupted careers, or familiar schools.


Replace “must have startup experience” with “can work independently as priorities change,” supported by evidence such as a project completed through changing requirements.


Define the selection rubric and rating criteria before reviewing applicants so a favored candidate doesn’t reshape the standards.


## Write Inclusive Job Descriptions


Separate day-one skills from teachable skills in plain language. State work hours, location expectations, and compensation range.


-


Replace “digital native” with “can build spreadsheet reports using pivot tables,” if accurate.


-


Replace “bachelor’s degree required” with “degree or equivalent practical experience” when either suffices, a common step in[diversity recruiting for startups](https://www.dover.com/blog/startup-diversity-hiring-guide) .


Provide an accommodation contact,[accessible application forms](https://www.w3.org/WAI/tutorials/forms/) , and a working request process alongside your equal-opportunity statement so candidates can act on the invitation.


## Broaden Sourcing Beyond Familiar Networks


Supplement referrals with outreach through community organizations, professional associations, and disability employment organizations. Include community colleges, apprenticeships, return-to-work programs, and re-entry programs, approaches worth weighing alongside other[considerations for supporting diversity](https://www.dover.com/blog/impact-hiring-3-things-to-consider-when-prioritizing-diversity) .


Ask employees to share openings beyond their closest professional circles. Keep opportunities broadly available and assess applicants against the same job-relevant criteria.


Track which channels bring qualified applicants and adjust outreach accordingly. Treat community partnerships as ongoing relationships, without promising demographic hiring outcomes.


Broader outreach takes recruiting hours that many founders do not have. An ATS can show which channels produce qualified applicants, but it does not do the outreach itself. When a role is specialized or no one on the team has bandwidth, a fractional recruiter working inside the same ATS can run community and association outreach against the criteria you already set, while your team keeps ownership of the hiring decision.


## Make Applications and Interviews Accessible


Test the candidate journey for keyboard navigation, screen-reader compatibility, accessible documents, and captions. Provide clear application instructions and alternatives for inaccessible steps.


Invite accommodation requests privately, following the Job Accommodation Network’s guidance on[reasonable accommodations in hiring](https://askjan.org/publications/employers/employers-guide-hiring-process.cfm) . Discuss accessible interview locations, flexible scheduling, or alternative assessment formats with the candidate, since[candidate experience in hiring](https://www.dover.com/blog/why-candidate-experience-matters-in-hiring) shapes whether they stay engaged through the process. Keep diagnosis details out of interviewer discussions; share only necessary arrangements. An equitable interview process measures the same underlying competency while allowing formats to vary with access needs.


## Screen Candidates Fairly and Review AI-Assisted Decisions


Apply the same rubric to every application, crediting transferable skills without treating names, home location, career gaps, or company prestige as shortcuts. Anonymized screening can hide identity cues, though work histories may reveal them.


For AI-assisted screening:


-


Check scoring criteria for job relevance.


-


Test for inappropriate exclusions and accessibility barriers.


-


Keep human reviewers responsible for checking recommendations and changing decisions.


Software scores prove neither suitability nor freedom from bias, which is one reason[candidate experience best practices](https://www.dover.com/blog/candidate-experience-guide-best-practices) call for human review at every stage.


## Build an Equitable Interview Process


Weight scorecard items by their importance to the role’s core responsibilities, giving required skills more influence than teachable preferences. Set those weights before interviews and apply them consistently across candidates.


-


Competency: resolving competing priorities.


-


Question: “Describe a time two urgent requests conflicted.”


-


Evidence standard: explains tradeoffs, decisions, and stakeholder communication.


Allow accommodations without changing the competency assessed. Replace “culture fit” with observable behaviors, like respectful disagreement, one of several[steps to reduce bias in hiring](https://www.dover.com/ebooks/building-a-hiring-process-steps-to-reduce-bias-and-get-organized) . Seek varied interviewer perspectives; panel composition alone cannot prevent bias.


## Train Hiring Teams to Apply Standards Consistently


Inclusive hiring training should include mock interviews, sample-answer scoring, and accommodation scenarios. Have interviewers compare ratings, explain discrepancies, ask relevant follow-ups, and record evidence using a consistent[interview scorecard](https://www.dover.com/blog/interview-scorecard-guide) . Attendance alone says little about how consistently they apply standards.


Assign a process owner to review feedback quality, challenge unsupported judgments, and document decision reasons. Give each interviewer a clear responsibility and repeat these checks for every role without adding committees.


## Assess Criminal Histories and Nontraditional Backgrounds in Context


Blanket assumptions about criminal records, career breaks, military transitions, or unconventional education can obscure relevant skills. Apply consistent, contextual standards; partnerships with transition and re-entry programs can broaden access while preserving the legitimate role requirements founders weigh when learning[how to interview candidates for a startup](https://www.dover.com/blog/how-to-interview-candidates-for-your-startup) .


Keep criminal-history screening separate from education and work-history review. Consider the record’s relevance to actual duties, as[EEOC arrest and conviction guidance](https://www.eeoc.gov/laws/guidance/enforcement-guidance-consideration-arrest-and-conviction-records-employment-decisions) outlines, and seek qualified legal review of jurisdiction-specific background-check and fair-chance hiring requirements before setting screening policies.


## Extend Inclusion Through Offers and Onboarding


Use consistent offer criteria and compensation bands, accessible offer documents, clear benefits explanations, and realistic response windows. Tie higher offers to documented experience and broader role scope, not negotiation confidence alone.


Extend inclusive hiring practices into onboarding: carry agreed accommodations forward, clarify workplace expectations, and provide access to mentorship and development. Recruitment alone cannot guarantee retention; inclusion also depends on what new hires experience after acceptance.


## Measure Hiring Equity Without Overinterpreting Small Samples


Track stage conversion, assessment outcomes, withdrawals, offer acceptance, and candidate feedback. Keep lawful, voluntary demographic collection separate from selection, a distinction covered in a broader[guide to interviewing](https://www.dover.com/ebooks/improve-interview-process) .


A selection rate below the[four-fifths threshold](https://www.eeoc.gov/laws/guidance/questions-and-answers-clarify-and-provide-common-interpretation-uniform-guidelines) relative to the highest group’s rate can signal potential adverse impact. With small startup samples, one decision can sharply change percentages; seek qualified review of patterns.


The threshold is neither a quota nor a legal safe harbor. Disparities prompt investigation, not automatic conclusions.


## An Inclusive Hiring Checklist and Guide Template


Build an inclusive hiring toolkit with:


-


Role-criteria worksheet


-


Job-description checklist


-


Accessibility review


-


Sourcing plan


-


Interview scorecard


-


Decision log


-


Process-review checklist


Use this template for each item:


Field Blank Fictional example


Item ___ Accessibility review


Owner ___ Sam


Evidence ___ Keyboard test passed


Barriers ___ Missing captions


Review date ___ October 12, 2026


Keep editable and on-page versions, plus an accessible, printable PDF.


## How Dover Supports a Consistent Inclusive Hiring Workflow


Dover’s free ATS supports inclusive hiring practices with customizable interview plans, structured feedback forms subject to plan limits, candidate notes, and unlimited jobs and users. Shared plans and recorded feedback can support consistency; your team remains responsible for accessibility, lawful criteria, and hiring judgments.


An ATS records candidates, interview plans, and feedback, but it does not source or screen candidates on its own. Teams hiring a few roles a year can often run an inclusive process with the ATS as their system of record. As hiring volume rises, a role gets harder to source, or no one has recruiting bandwidth, a fractional recruiter can plug in on top of the same ATS to handle sourcing, screening, and coordination using your interview plans and scorecards.


Because the recruiter and hiring team share one pipeline, both see the same candidate stages and feedback, which can reduce duplicate outreach and keep assessment criteria consistent. The average cost per hire across all roles on Dover is $4,800, though costs vary by role complexity and recruiter, and there are no long-term contracts. Neither software nor recruiter support guarantees equitable outcomes.


## FAQs


### If your team has one afternoon, what inclusive hiring practices should you set up first?


Start with one role’s job-relevant criteria, interview questions, and evidence standards, not a company-wide policy rewrite. Add those standards to your interview plan and structured feedback forms. Assign someone to test the application journey and handle accommodation requests before applications open.


### What should you do if your interviewers record conflicting ratings?


Review the evidence behind each rating before averaging scores or taking a vote. Ask interviewers to connect their feedback to the agreed competency standards; if evidence is missing, consider a focused follow-up that follows the same assessment rules for comparable candidates. Record the decision reason in candidate notes so disagreement does not disappear into an unexplained score.


### How do you keep an inclusive hiring guide PDF consistent with your interview plans?


Treat the PDF as a dated reference copy and keep one editable guide as your source of truth. Assign an owner to update both the guide and the relevant interview plans whenever criteria change, recording the revision date. For an active search, document whether any change requires earlier candidates to be reassessed against the same standards.


### Do you need a recruiter if you already use an ATS for inclusive hiring?


An ATS organizes your process, including interview plans, structured feedback, and candidate notes, but it does not source or screen candidates by itself. Founders hiring a few roles a year can often run inclusive hiring with an ATS alone. A fractional recruiter becomes worth considering when hiring volume climbs, a role is hard to source, or no one has time for broader outreach. Fractional recruiters can work inside the same ATS, so they follow your rubric and scorecards while your team makes the hiring decisions. Some teams pair a free ATS with on-demand fractional recruiters in one shared system, as Dover does.


## Final Thoughts on Inclusive Recruitment


You don’t need more committees to make hiring fairer. Clear criteria give your team a shared starting point for each role. From there, fairness tends to come from small, repeatable habits: scoring every candidate against the same rubric, recording the evidence behind each rating, and checking where qualified people drop out of your funnel. A five-person startup and a fifty-person team will apply these differently. Dover’s free ATS, for instance, is built with customizable interview plans and structured feedback forms, which gives a small team one place to keep criteria and ratings together. The[inclusive hiring practices](https://www.dover.com/) that hold up are the ones your team can keep running as hiring picks up.
